prompt.context: Our client is a pharmaceutical company that has developed a remedy for female balding. The drug has cleared a lengthy and delayed testing process. The drug will be off patent in five years. Before initiating drug production, the client wants us to determine whether the drug will be profitable and whether or not to go ahead with production.
prompt.question: Should the client go ahead with production? Is the drug profitable? After completing the profitability analysis, you will also be asked to recommend a launch strategy based on market research about two possible product formulations.

clarifying_info.q: What did the client spend on testing?
What is the price of the drug?
clarifying_info.a: The price is comparable to the existing substitute at $2,000 per treatment; one treatment is needed per year.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a comparable substitute on the market?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. One comparable substitute currently exists. Once the client's drug enters the market, both products will divide market share equally. Both have no comparative advantage over the other and will charge the same price.

clarifying_info.q: What happens to market share after the patent expires?
clarifying_info.a: Post-patent expiry, the client's share will shrink to 20% of its pre-patent expiry share.

clarifying_info.q: What age group is affected by female balding?
clarifying_info.a: Average woman starts balding at age 40. Between ages 30-40 the drug has some preventative benefits. Starting at age 60, even the most effective drugs cannot remedy female balding.

clarifying_info.q: Is the drug covered by health insurance?
clarifying_info.a: Payment for the product is not covered by most health insurance plans.

clarifying_info.q: Is there any current market size data?
clarifying_info.a: No information on current market size is available; you should size the overall market and the client's market share.

exhibits.title: Chart 1: Customer Survey — Importance of Product Characteristic by Age Cohort
exhibits.shows: A radar/spider chart showing ratings (scale 0–5) for three product characteristics — Effectiveness, Convenience/Ease of Use, and Cost — across three age cohorts: 30–40, 40–50, and 50–60.

data.note: Chart is provided only during the launch strategy portion of the case, after the profitability recommendation is made.

framework: Define the problem: go/no go decision on drug production — requires profitability analysis (revenue vs. costs over the patent lifecycle)
Revenue: size the total addressable market (# of interested and able-to-pay women), apply market share assumptions, multiply by price
Costs: identify which costs are relevant (exclude sunk cost of $8B testing); annual operating costs = production + marketing & sales + distribution
Profitability: compare annual revenue vs. annual costs, both pre-patent and post-patent expiry
Risks and other considerations: competitive response, market share erosion, cost variability, international markets
Launch strategy (second part): match formulations to customer segments using the market research exhibit

questions.prompt: Size the total market: how many women are potential buyers of this drug?
questions.guidance: Strong answer walks through: US population ~300M, ~50% female = 150M (can round to 160M for ease). Segment by age: only women 30-60 are relevant (30-40 preventive benefit, 40-60 primary benefit, 60+ ineffective). Estimate % interested by age bracket, then filter by affordability at $2,000/treatment. Final answer should be ~10M women who are both interested and able to pay.

math.setup: US female population ~160M, split evenly into 10-year brackets of ~20M each. Apply % interested: 0% for 0-30, 20-40% for 30-40, 30-60% for 40-60, 0% for 60+. Revised assumption: 20% of 30-40 and 30% of 40-60 interested. Then filter by affordability (income split 20% low / 60% middle / 20% upper; % able to pay: 20% low, 60% middle, 100% upper).
steps: Women aged 30-40: 20M x 20% interested = 4M — but sample uses lower revised rate: 20M x 20% = 4M (wait, sample analysis revised: 20% of 30-40 = 4M, then affordability applied)
Affordability filter on 16M: 20% low income = 3.2M x 20% able = 0.64M ≈ 0.6M; 60% middle = 9.6M x 60% able = 5.76M ≈ 6M; 20% upper = 3.2M x 100% = 3.2M ≈ 3M
Client's market share (split equally with one competitor): 10M / 2 = 5M women

questions.guidance: Revenue = target population x price per treatment x frequency. Use 5M women at $2,000/treatment/year.

questions.prompt: Calculate annual costs (exclude the $8B testing spend). Is the drug profitable pre-patent expiry?
questions.guidance: Candidate must identify $8B testing as a sunk cost and exclude it. Annual costs = production + marketing & sales + distribution = $1B + $2.5B + $0.8B = $4.3B/year. Annual profit pre-patent = $10B - $4.3B = $5.7B.

math.setup: Annual costs = Production + Marketing & Sales + Distribution (exclude $8B sunk cost of testing)
math.answer: Annual profit of $5.7B pre-patent expiry; the $8B testing cost is a sunk cost and must NOT be included

questions.prompt: Calculate annual revenue and profitability post-patent expiry.
questions.guidance: Post-patent, client's market share falls to 20% of pre-patent share. Pre-patent share was 50% of total market (5M of 10M). Post-patent share = 20% x 50% = 10% of total market = 1M women. Revenue post-patent = 1M x $2,000 = $2B/year. Costs remain $4.3B/year (assumed constant), so the drug is unprofitable post-patent at current pricing.

math.setup: Post-patent share = 20% of pre-patent client share. Pre-patent client served 5M. Post-patent: 5M x 20% = 1M women.
math.answer: Post-patent annual loss of ~$2.3B at current pricing; profitability depends on cost reduction or market share gains

questions.prompt: After completing the profitability analysis, the client received approval for two formulations. Using the market research chart, recommend which formulation(s) to launch: Formulation 1 (once-daily, less effective, lower price) or Formulation 2 (twice-daily, most effective, higher price).
questions.guidance: Candidate should read the radar chart to identify which product characteristics each age cohort values most, then match to formulations. Formulation 1 (convenience + cost) suits the 40-50 and 50-60 segments. Formulation 2 (effectiveness) suits the 30-40 segment. Candidate may recommend either or both, but must provide clear rationale and acknowledge risks of launching both (branding complexity, cannibalization, resource allocation).

brainstorming.prompt: What are the key risks and factors that could affect profitability beyond the base case?

categories.name: Competitive Dynamics
ideas: Competitor lowers price to gain share, eroding client's revenue
Competitor's drug goes off-patent before the five-year window ends, accelerating market share erosion
New entrants enter the attractive, relatively unmet market (only 2 products currently)

categories.name: Cost Variability
ideas: Production, marketing, and distribution costs assumed constant but will vary with volume and promotional scope
Marketing budget of $2.5B/year may be insufficient to build consumer awareness of a novel product category

categories.name: Market Sizing Assumptions
ideas: Actual % of women interested or able to pay may differ significantly
Consumer awareness of the product could limit actual uptake
Insurance coverage could expand (upside) or remain negligible (downside)

categories.name: Strategic Options Post-Patent
ideas: Lower price post-patent to maintain profitable market share
Expand to international markets where US testing is accepted
Target adjacent segments: men experiencing hair loss, or different hair-loss indications

recommendation: The client should proceed with drug production for the next five years; at $5.7B annual profit pre-patent expiry the drug is clearly profitable in the near term
Post-patent profitability is uncertain at current pricing and costs; the decision to continue production after year five requires updated market sizing and a cost/pricing review

For launch strategy, the client should launch Formulation 1 (once-daily, lower price) as the primary product, targeting women aged 40-60 who prioritize convenience and cost; this is the larger segment and generates more near-term revenue

The client should not launch both formulations simultaneously at launch due to branding complexity, risk of cannibalization, and limited marketing resources; Formulation 2 can be considered later as a premium extension
risks: Market share and price assumptions could be disrupted by an aggressive competitive response
Cost structure may not remain constant; if costs rise faster than revenue, profitability narrows
The marketing budget may be insufficient to educate a largely unaware customer base about a novel product
Post-patent, unless costs are reduced or market share actively defended, production becomes loss-making
Launching only Formulation 1 foregoes the younger 30-40 cohort willing to pay more for effectiveness — a higher-lifetime-value segment
next_steps: Model sensitivity of profitability to key assumptions (% interested, affordability, competitive pricing)
Assess whether marketing budget is sufficient for market education and what return on incremental spend looks like
Evaluate international market opportunity where US clinical trials would be accepted
Develop a post-patent pricing and cost optimization roadmap
Post-launch of Formulation 1, evaluate feasibility of Formulation 2 as a premium SKU once brand is established
